Historical observations for this pairing are based on satellite observations collected daily. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and the Rutgers University Global Snow Lab processed the data and calculated weekly average snow-covered area. EPA calculated seasonal and annual averages. While some satellite records are available for earlier years, 1981 was the first year with sufficient records analyzed using the latest methods.

Model outputs are based on a set of 13 global climate models that reflect scientists’ current understanding of how greenhouse gases warm the atmosphere; how this heat moves between the atmosphere, water, and land; and how these changes influence the air temperatures that allow snow to fall and stay on the ground. These same 13 models were part of the set of 16 used in the most recent National Climate Assessment. (The other three models did not include snow cover.) The modeled lines are smoother than the historical trends because the project team averaged 13 models together and also applied an 11-year smoothing filter, both of which smooth out year-to-year variability. However, the shaded bands do include year-to-year variability.

In an initial comparison between observed and modeled data, the models underestimated actual snow cover year-round and in all seasons. This may be due to the differences in grid sizes between the model and the observations (see technical documentation). The project team corrected this bias by shifting all model outputs by a consistent amount for each season so each model hindcast would align with average observed results for the years where they coincide, 1981–2014.
